The funeral services industry in the United States — funeral homes, crematoriums and cemeteries — generates about $15 billion in annual revenues, according to the 2012 “Funeral Services” report from Research and Markets. Some companies in the industry have a poor [[1]] for consumer abuses, but the services continue to be necessary for virtually every family. Problem areas in the industry [[2]] high costs, fraudulent prepaid funeral plans, high-pressure casket sales, and sales of unnecessary products.
Some firms market prepaid funeral plans as an affordable way for families to provide for the end-of-life needs of parents or others. Having a way for consumers to pay the current price in monthly installments for a future funeral might be viewed as a well-intentioned prevention against price [[3]]. Some consumer advocates, however, have been charging plan providers with abuses including fraud and mismanagement. Some consumers have [[4]] being deceived when they canceled their contracts. An alternative to purchasing a prepaid funeral plan is to consult with an attorney about establishing a [[5]] to fund a future funeral and burial.
The Federal Trade Commission’s Funeral Rule requires funeral homes to provide families with a price list of caskets and other items. In violation of this requirement, some unethical establishments have [[6]] emotional family members by showing the most expensive caskets before showing more affordable models. Besides, many families are unaware of the funeral homes’ obligation to allow the use of caskets purchased elsewhere, without any [[7]] to the customer. In addition, some funeral homes have used high-pressure tactics to sell [[8]] items at inflated prices.
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) enacted the Funeral Rule in 1984. The FTC designed it to protect consumers by requiring that funeral providers give them [[9]] information about the goods and services they might purchase from them. The Funeral Rule [[10]] consumers the right to choose only the goods and services they want and to pay only for those they select. General features of the rule include consumers’ rights to obtain price quotations in writing and to obtain full disclosure of pricing. The Funeral Rule provides for nearly every possible transaction between funeral providers and consumers.
